name: Hair relaxer / chemical straightener
lead: A hair relaxer, or chemical straightener, is a cosmetic product that permanently loosens tight curls or straightens hair by breaking the bonds that hold its shape; new growth returns to its natural texture.[1][2] Relaxers are almost always alkaline: lye relaxers use sodium hydroxide, and no-lye versions use other alkalis such as calcium, potassium or guanidine hydroxide, while others use thioglycolate or sulfite-based chemistry.[1][2]

Early products date to 1909, when Garrett Augustus Morgan developed a straightening cream, with commercial lye relaxers appearing in 1917.[2] Use is especially prevalent among Black women in the United States.[3]

Research on health effects is active. Large cohort studies in the Black Women's Health Study examined relaxer use and uterine fibroids, breast cancer and uterine cancer, with differing findings, and the FDA proposed in 2023 to ban formaldehyde in hair relaxers.[2][3][4][5]

paras: Chemical relaxers break disulfide bonds that give hair its curl, leaving it straighter; lye formulations at roughly 5 to 10 percent sodium hydroxide have a pH around 10 to 14.[1][2] Thioglycolate-based products must be neutralized afterward, and sulfite products work more slowly with less irritation.[2] Relaxers differ from temporary heat straightening and from keratin treatments.[1]

A 2012 Black Women's Health Study analysis of 23,580 premenopausal women examined relaxer use, including burns and formulation, in relation to uterine fibroids.[3] A 2007 analysis from the same cohort reported that relaxers were not associated with breast cancer risk,[4] while a 2023 study of 44,798 women examined uterine cancer risk.[5] A separate NIH-linked study, as summarized on Wikipedia, found nearly double the risk of uterine cancer in frequent users compared with non-users; these are observational associations.[2][1]

Other studies have examined fecundability in a North American preconception cohort, preterm birth among African-American women, and circulating estrogens in women in Ghana.[6][7][8] A 2013 article in the International Journal of Trichology asks whether adverse effects of chemical relaxers are myth or reality.[9]

Relaxers can cause scalp burns, dermatitis, brittle hair, breakage and hair loss.[2] Case literature includes caustic ingestion and a deep infection complicating irritant dermatitis from a relaxer.[10][11]

The FDA does not approve cosmetics before sale and full ingredient disclosure is not mandatory; in 2023 it proposed banning formaldehyde in hair relaxers.[2] The Rio Hair Naturalizer System, marketed as chemical-free in the 1990s, led to a class action over scalp damage and hair loss and was withdrawn, and more recent lawsuits accuse manufacturers of failing to disclose formaldehyde-related risks.[2]
In forum threads about keratin treatments, relaxers are mentioned by users as a stronger straightening alternative.[12]
No randomized trials of relaxers for appearance were found. Human observational studies of health outcomes are summarized under Health research.[3][4][5][6][7][8]

card.summary: Alkaline chemical straightening of curly hair; effective cosmetically, with ongoing cancer and fibroid research and burn risks.
card.aka: Lye relaxer, no-lye relaxer, chemical hair straightener
card.note: Observational studies link frequent use with uterine cancer; scalp burns are documented.

quick.overview:
Hair relaxers permanently loosen curls or straighten hair using alkaline or thioglycolate chemistry. New growth returns to its natural texture, so treatments are repeated.

Most research concerns health outcomes in Black women, where studies report differing findings across fibroids, breast cancer and uterine cancer.
quick.mechanism: The chemicals swell the hair shaft and break the disulfide bonds that hold its curl, so hair sets straighter.
quick.risks: Documented harms include scalp burns, dermatitis, breakage and hair loss. Observational studies have linked frequent use to higher uterine cancer risk, and the FDA proposed banning formaldehyde in relaxers in 2023. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by the FDA.
